questions.prompt: A real-world object, such as a light pole on campus, is called an:
questions.explain: Entities are the real things; features are how we represent them in data.

questions.prompt: When an entity is put on a map or in a database, it becomes a:
questions.explain: A feature is a simplified representation of an entity.

questions.prompt: Data abstraction is:
choices: The process of making the real world readable by a computer
Converting a raster to a vector
questions.explain: It runs from the real world, through a data model and a data structure, down to 0s and 1s.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a data model and a data structure?
choices: The model is the idea of what to keep; the structure is how it is laid out in memory or on disk
Models are for rasters and structures for vectors
The structure is chosen before the model
questions.explain: The data model decides what to keep (wetlands with an ID, area, type); the data structure organizes it as coordinates and tables.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of continuous data?
questions.explain: Continuous data have a value everywhere, changing from place to place.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a discrete object?
questions.explain: Discrete objects are present in one place and absent in another, with clear edges.

questions.prompt: Which data model is best for discrete objects such as parcels and wells?
questions.explain: Vector data store discrete features precisely as coordinates.

questions.prompt: Which data model is best for continuous surfaces such as elevation?
questions.explain: A raster's grid gives every location a value.

questions.prompt: A building can be stored as a line (its outline) or as an area (a polygon). What does the polygon add?
choices: Enclosure: it knows it has an inside
questions.explain: A polygon encloses space, so you can measure its area or test whether a point is inside it.

questions.prompt: A large-scale map, such as 1:10,000, shows a large area with little detail.
questions.explain: Large scale means a large fraction, so a small area in a lot of detail. A small-scale map shows a large area.

questions.prompt: On a map of the whole country, a city is drawn as a point instead of an area. This is called:
questions.explain: At smaller scales, detail has to go, and features may change geometry.

questions.prompt: A building's name and the year it was built are its:
questions.explain: Attributes are non-spatial information about a spatial feature.

questions.prompt: Class grades are an example of spatial data.
questions.explain: Grades have no location of their own, so they are non-spatial data.

questions.prompt: The start or end point of a line is called a:
questions.explain: Nodes are where lines start and end, and where networks connect.

questions.prompt: A point in the middle of a line, where it changes direction, is called a:
questions.explain: Vertices give a line its shape. More vertices mean a smoother line and a bigger file.

questions.prompt: Why do thematic layers stack exactly on top of each other?
choices: They were made by the same person
questions.explain: A shared coordinate system makes the layers line up, so a map is just layers drawn together.

questions.prompt: A raster stores the location of each cell by:
choices: The coordinates of its origin, plus the cell size and each cell's row and column
A pair of coordinates for every cell
questions.explain: Any cell's location can be worked out from the origin and the cell size.

questions.prompt: You change a raster from 50 m cells to 25 m cells over the same area. How does the number of cells change?
choices: It is four times as many
questions.explain: Halving the cell size halves both the width and the height of each cell, so each old cell becomes 2 × 2 = 4 cells.

questions.prompt: A raster has 30 m cells, and its lower-left corner is at northing `3950000`. Store the northing of the cell in row 4 (counting up from 0) in a variable called `n_cell`.
questions.solution:
northing_ll <- 3950000
cell_size <- 30
row <- 4
n_cell <- northing_ll + row * cell_size
questions.explain: N = N lower-left + row × cell size = 3,950,000 + 4 × 30 = 3,950,120.

questions.prompt: A raster covers an area 3,000 m wide and 2,000 m tall with 10 m cells. Store the total number of cells in a variable called `n_cells`.
questions.solution:
width <- 3000
height <- 2000
cell_size <- 10
n_cells <- (width / cell_size) * (height / cell_size)
questions.explain: 300 columns × 200 rows = 60,000 cells.

questions.prompt: Which file in a shapefile holds the attribute table?
questions.explain: `.shp` holds geometry, `.shx` an index, `.dbf` the attributes, and `.prj` the projection.

questions.prompt: Which shapefile file tells the software the coordinate system?
questions.explain: Without the `.prj`, the software can't place the data correctly on the Earth.

questions.prompt: A `.shp` file on its own, without its other files, is a complete, usable shapefile.
questions.explain: At least `.shp`, `.shx`, and `.dbf` are needed. Keep (and zip) all the files together.

questions.prompt: In GeoJSON, which coordinate comes first?
questions.explain: GeoJSON writes longitude, then latitude, in WGS84.

questions.prompt: Which format is behind Google Earth?
questions.explain: KML, Keyhole Markup Language, is XML-based. A `.kmz` is a zipped KML.

questions.prompt: Which format is the standard for raster data such as satellite images?
questions.explain: A GeoTIFF is a TIFF image with its location stored inside the file.

questions.prompt: Metadata are:
choices: Data about the data: who made it, when, how, and how accurate it is
The largest values in a dataset
questions.explain: Without metadata you can't judge whether data fit your purpose. US federal data follow the FGDC standard.
